text:
The three days of travel in Genesis 22 stand as a kind of suspended sentence. Outwardly nothing happens; in significance everything happens. The servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire receive the stress of the account; the instruments of the act are named before the act itself occurs. Obedience and horror are held together, and neither is suffered to prevail. Faith here is a structured relation, rather than a feeling.

Placed beside the earlier promise, the difference between promise and scene narrows. Isaac is still the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; and the chapter turns that covenant promise into a test. The scene hinges on the single word _hineni_, "here I am," spoken by Abraham three times, first to God, then to Isaac, then to the angel. Each utterance bears another meaning, and each costs more. Presence, in this story, has the language of loss.
